Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), Clause 17.5.2, sentence (1) states that when an IRS is in operation, the system in operation shall decide on any line call challenge, unless it gives an inconsistent or obviously incorrect decision, in which case the Referee instructs the Umpire how to proceed. Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), Clause 2.4.2, sentence (1) repeats that the IRS shall be used to decide any line call challenge (Law 17.5.2). ITTO Clause 5.8.6 (1) adds that the IRS reviews the original decision and indicates the result as "IN", "OUT" or "NO DECISION". ITTO Clause 5.8.10 covers the inconsistent/obviously incorrect exception (Referee instructs the Umpire). Related but not answering the part directly: ITTO 5.8.9 (1) (a "NO DECISION" is a "Let" if the original call was "Unsighted", otherwise the original challenged decision stands) and ITTO 8.2 (2) (the result of a challenge where IRS is in operation supersedes the original line call).
answer.answer:
When an Instant Review System is in operation, the system in operation itself decides on any line call challenge (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 17.5.2; Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 2.4.2) — it reviews the original decision and indicates the result of the challenge as either "IN", "OUT" or "NO DECISION" (ITTO Clause 5.8.6). The only exception: if the system gives an inconsistent or obviously incorrect decision, the Referee shall instruct the Umpire how to proceed (Law 17.5.2).
ITTO Clause 5.8.10: if the IRS indicates an inconsistent (e.g. between text and graphic) or obviously incorrect decision, the Umpire calls the Referee before the next rally and the Referee instructs the Umpire how to proceed. ITTO Clause 5.8.9: if the IRS indicates "NO DECISION", it is a "Let" if the original call was "Unsighted", otherwise the original challenged decision stands. ITTO Clause 8.2: the result of a challenge where an IRS is in operation supersedes the original line call by the Line Judge.

question: A player misbehaves during the interval. Is that treated differently from misconduct during a game?

answer.reasoning: The question has one part: whether misconduct during an interval is treated differently from misconduct during a game. The Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, clause 5.17.6 answers it directly: sentence (1) states misconduct during intervals (Law 16.2) is treated as misconduct during a game, and sentence (2) adds that the standard misconduct call should be made immediately on occurrence. Clauses 5.17.7 and 5.17.8 bear on the question (what the Umpire calls after the interval when a warning or fault was issued) without answering it, so they go in related_sentences.
answer.answer:
No. Under Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, clause 5.17.6, misconduct during intervals (Law 16.2) is treated as misconduct during a game, and it should be followed with the call as in Instructions 5.17.3, 5.17.4 or 5.17.5 immediately on occurrence of the misconduct.
Instructions 5.17.7 and 5.17.8 (ITTO 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26) say that if misconduct during an interval led to a warning (Law 16.7.1.1) or a fault (Law 16.7.1.2 or 16.7.1.3), the Umpire makes the corresponding announcement after the interval.
